title: SMTP Extension for Internationalized Email
summary: This RFC specifies an SMTP extension for transporting and delivering email messages that have internationalized email addresses or header information.

plainLanguage.summary: Email addresses used to be restricted to plain ASCII characters. RFC 6531 adds an SMTP extension called SMTPUTF8 so that servers can agree to carry addresses and headers written in UTF-8. A sending server asks for the extension first, and the receiving server advertises it in its greeting reply.

questions: how to send email to unicode address
how does smtp support unicode email addresses
what happens if a server does not support smtputf8
subtitle: The SMTP extension that lets mail servers agree to carry non-ASCII addresses and UTF-8 headers.

tldr.problem: SMTP envelopes and mailbox names were defined entirely in ASCII, so addresses with non-ASCII local parts or internationalized domain names could not be sent.
tldr.mechanism: Servers advertise a new EHLO keyword, SMTPUTF8. A client then adds an SMTPUTF8 parameter to MAIL, and UTF-8 may appear in mailbox names, in the headers defined by RFC 6532 and in a few replies.
tldr.outcome: It replaces the experimental approach in RFC 5336 and is a Proposed Standard. A client must not send an internationalized message to a server that does not offer the extension.

today: RFC 6531 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2012. It obsoletes RFC 5336, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It works together with RFC 6532, which defines the header format.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The document defines a Simple Mail Transfer Protocol extension so that servers can advertise the ability to accept and process internationalized email addresses and internationalized email headers. An extended overview of the extension model for internationalized email addresses and email headers is given in RFC 6530, referred to as the framework document.

The specification extends some syntax rules defined in RFC 5321 and permits internationalized email addresses in the envelope and in trace fields, but it does not modify RFC 5321. It permits data formats defined in RFC 6532, but it does not modify RFC 5322. It does require that the 8BITMIME extension be announced by the SMTPUTF8-aware SMTP server and used with BODY=8BITMIME by the SMTPUTF8-aware SMTP client, but it does not modify the 8BITMIME specification in any way.

This specification replaces an earlier, experimental, approach to the same problem, RFC 5336. Section 6 of the framework document describes the changes in approach between the two, and anyone converting an implementation from the experimental specification needs to review those changes carefully.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC takes the experimental SMTPUTF8 work and turns it into a standard. It does not rewrite basic SMTP; it adds one keyword and one parameter.

sections.title: Framework for the Internationalization Extension
sections.content:
The service extension is named Internationalized Email, and the EHLO keyword value associated with it is SMTPUTF8. No parameter values are defined for that keyword, and in order to permit future extensions the EHLO response MUST NOT contain any parameters for it. A client that is SMTPUTF8-aware MUST ignore any parameters if they appear, and a server that includes SMTPUTF8 in its EHLO response MUST be fully compliant with this version of the specification.

One optional parameter, SMTPUTF8, is added to the MAIL command. It does not accept a value. Its presence asserts that the envelope includes a non-ASCII address, that the message being sent is an internationalized message, or that the message needs SMTPUTF8 support. The maximum length of a MAIL command line is increased by 10 characters to allow for the parameter. One optional SMTPUTF8 parameter is also added to the VERIFY and EXPAND commands, indicating that the client can accept Unicode characters in UTF-8 encoding in the replies.

No additional SMTP verbs are defined. Servers offering this extension MUST provide support for and announce the 8BITMIME extension. The reverse-path and forward-path of the MAIL and RCPT commands are extended to allow Unicode characters encoded in UTF-8 in mailbox names, and the message body is extended as specified in RFC 6532. The extension is valid on the submission port and may also be used with the Local Mail Transfer Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole extension is one word in the server's hello, plus one flag on the command that starts a mail transfer. It changes no verbs and adds no new ones.

sections.title: The SMTPUTF8 Extension
sections.content:
A server that announces the SMTPUTF8 extension must be prepared to accept a UTF-8 string anywhere RFC 5321 allows a mailbox to appear. Although the local part may contain non-ASCII characters, the parsing of the local part and the delimiters used are unchanged from the base email specification. Any domain name looked up in the DNS must conform to and be processed as specified for Internationalizing Domain Names in Applications, so the client or server must either use a Unicode-aware DNS library or transform the internationalized domain name to A-label form, a fully qualified domain name containing one or more A-labels but no U-labels.

A client that receives the SMTPUTF8 keyword in response to EHLO may transmit mailbox names as internationalized strings in UTF-8 form, may send a UTF-8 header, and may transmit the domain parts of mailbox names as A-labels or U-labels. The presence of the extension does not change the server-relaying behaviours described in RFC 5321.

If the extension is not offered by the server, the client MUST NOT transmit an internationalized email address and MUST NOT transmit a message containing internationalized mail headers at any level within its MIME structure. An internationalized domain name in A-label form is not considered internationalized for this purpose. If a client attempts to transfer an internationalized message and meets a server without the extension, a message submission agent may transform the message, since the wide discretion allowed by RFC 6409 permits changing addresses. Otherwise the client SHOULD reject the message, either during the SMTP transaction or afterwards with a non-delivery notification that conforms to RFC 5321, RFC 3464 and RFC 6533. The client may also requeue the message and try later or try an alternate MX host.

For all other cases, and for addresses and messages that do not need the extension, SMTPUTF8-aware clients and servers do not change the behaviour specified in RFC 5321.
sections.plainLanguage: If the server says it supports SMTPUTF8, the client may write addresses in UTF-8. If it does not, the client must not send a message that needs it, and must either fix the message up or refuse it.

sections.title: Extended Mailbox Address Syntax
sections.content:
RFC 5321 defines the syntax of a mailbox entirely in terms of ASCII characters. This document extends that rule to support non-ASCII characters. The mailbox rule is imported from RFC 5321 and updated, and other related rules are imported from RFC 5321, RFC 5234, RFC 5890 and RFC 6532 or are extended here.

The definition of sub-domain is extended to permit both the RFC 5321 definition and a UTF-8 string in a DNS label that conforms with the IDNA definitions. The definition of atext is extended to permit both the RFC 5321 definition and a UTF-8 string, and that string MUST NOT contain any of the ASCII graphics or control characters.

The rules that are updated directly or indirectly are Mailbox, Local-part, Dot-string, Quoted-string, QcontentSMTP, Domain and Atom. The UTF8-non-ascii rule is imported directly from RFC 6532, the DQUOTE rule from RFC 5234, and the U-label rule from RFC 5890.
sections.plainLanguage: The address grammar keeps its old ASCII forms and gains UTF-8 alternatives. The delimiters that separate the local part from the domain stay exactly as they were.

sections.title: MAIL Command Parameter Usage
sections.content:
If the envelope or message being sent requires the capabilities of the SMTPUTF8 extension, the client MUST supply the SMTPUTF8 parameter with the MAIL command, and the parameter must not accept a value. If the client knows that neither the envelope nor the message needs any of the extension's capabilities, it SHOULD NOT supply the parameter.

Because there is no guarantee that a next-hop server will support the extension, use of it always carries a risk of transmission failure, and during the early stages of deployment that risk will be quite high. There is therefore a distinct near-term advantage for ASCII-only messages to be sent without using the extension. The long-term advantage of casting ASCII characters as UTF-8 is that it permits pure-Unicode environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Only add the flag when the message really needs it. Plain ASCII mail sent without the flag is more likely to get through, because every server along the way understands it.

sections.title: Reply Codes for Non-ASCII Addresses
sections.content:
An SMTPUTF8-aware client MUST NOT send an internationalized message to a server that does not support SMTPUTF8. When messages are rejected because the RCPT command requires an ASCII address, the reply code 553 is returned with the meaning mailbox name not allowed. When they are rejected because the MAIL command requires an ASCII address, the reply code 550 is returned with the meaning mailbox unavailable. When the server supports enhanced mail system status codes, reply code X.6.7 is used, meaning non-ASCII addresses not permitted for that sender or recipient.

If a message is rejected after the final dot of the DATA command because one or more recipients cannot accept and process a message with internationalized email headers, the reply code 554 is used with the meaning transaction failed, and the enhanced reply code X.6.9 is used when the server supports them, meaning a UTF-8 header message cannot be transmitted to one or more recipients so the message must be rejected. Servers are encouraged to detect that recipients cannot accept internationalized messages and generate an error after the RCPT command rather than waiting until after the DATA command.
sections.plainLanguage: Each way of saying no has its own code. 553 and 550 mean the address was not allowed; 554 means the message was fine but a recipient could not handle it.

sections.title: UTF-8 Strings in Replies
sections.content:
If a client sends MAIL commands containing the SMTPUTF8 parameter, the server is permitted to use UTF-8 characters in the email address associated with the 251 and 551 reply codes, and the client MUST be able to accept and process them. If a MAIL command does not include the parameter, the server MUST NOT return a 251 or 551 response containing a non-ASCII mailbox, and MUST transform such responses into 250 or 550 responses that do not contain non-ASCII addresses.

If the SMTPUTF8 parameter is transmitted with the VERIFY and EXPAND commands, it indicates that the client can accept UTF-8 strings in the replies to those commands, and it SHOULD only be used after the client has seen the EHLO response carrying the SMTPUTF8 keyword. If a reply requires a UTF-8 string but the client did not use the parameter, the server MUST use either reply code 252, meaning cannot verify user but will accept the message and attempt the delivery, or 550, meaning requested action not taken, mailbox unavailable. The enhanced reply code X.6.8 is used when the server supports them, meaning a reply containing a UTF-8 string is required to show the mailbox name but that form of response is not permitted by the client.

A successful response MAY include the full name of the user and MUST include the mailbox of the user, in the form of a user name followed by the mailbox in angle brackets, or the mailbox on its own. Servers MUST NOT include non-ASCII characters in replies except in the cases specifically permitted in this section.
sections.plainLanguage: Replies normally stay in ASCII. A server may only put a non-ASCII address in a reply when the client asked for it, either by sending MAIL with the flag or by adding the flag to VERIFY and EXPAND.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extended security considerations discussion in the framework document applies here. The RFC adds a further point: internationalized email addresses will show up inside other systems, in particular the logging systems of SMTP transactions and other logs used to monitor the email systems, and the trouble ticket systems that security teams use to manage security incidents when an email address is involved.

In order to avoid problems that could cause loss of data, these systems will likely need extending to support full UTF-8, or an adequate mechanism for mapping non-ASCII strings to ASCII will need to be provided. Another security aspect is the ability of security team members to quickly understand, read and identify email addresses from logs when tracking an incident. Mechanisms to automatically and quickly provide the origin or ownership of an internationalized email address SHALL be implemented for use by log readers that cannot easily read non-ASCII information.
sections.plainLanguage: Non-ASCII addresses end up in log files and in incident reports, so the tools that read them have to cope with UTF-8 too, or be able to fall back to an ASCII form.

items.desc: A recipient cannot accept a message with internationalized headers.

items.desc: Used when a reply would need a UTF-8 string that the client did not ask for.

items.label: NON-ASCII ADDRESSES NOT PERMITTED
items.desc: Enhanced status code for a MAIL or RCPT command with a non-ASCII address.

items.label: UTF-8 REPLY REQUIRED BUT NOT PERMITTED
items.desc: Enhanced status code used when a UTF-8 string is needed but not allowed.

items.desc: Enhanced status code used when the message must be rejected after the DATA command.
